# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# cu_python_task - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cu-python-task/1.0.0/cu_python_task/

## Expand description

Python-backed Copper tasks.

This crate exists for rapid algorithm prototyping, not for production realtime robotics.

A [ PyTask](https://docs.rs/struct.PyTask.html) lets Copper keep ownership of scheduling, logging, replay, and task
lifecycle while delegating one task’s algorithm body to a Python function:

```
def process(ctx, input, state, output):
    ...
```
Two execution modes are available:

- `PyTaskMode::Process`- `CuHandle<CuSharedMemoryBuffer<T>>`, the handle is exported by descriptor so Python can read or write the underlying shared-memory bytes without copying them through CBOR.
- `PyTaskMode::Embedded`

Both modes are fundamentally at odds with Copper’s design center: predictable low-latency execution with minimal allocation on the realtime path. Using Python here will increase latency, jitter, and allocation pressure enough to ruin the realtime characteristics of the stack. Compared to a native Rust Copper task, the performance is abysmal.

The intended workflow is narrow:

- prototype one task quickly in Python
- stabilize the algorithm
- rewrite it in Rust, optionally using an LLM-assisted translation as a first draft

Do not treat Python tasks as a normal production integration path.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [PyTask](https://docs.rs/struct.PyTask.html)
- A Copper task whose `process(...)`implementation is provided by a Python script.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [PyInput](https://docs.rs/trait.PyInputSpec.html)- Spec
- Describes how a Python-backed task receives its Copper inputs.
- [PyOutput](https://docs.rs/trait.PyOutputSpec.html)- Spec
- Describes how a Python-backed task exposes Copper outputs.
- [PyTask](https://docs.rs/trait.PyTaskState.html)- State
- State carried across invocations of a `PyTask`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [PyUnary](https://docs.rs/type.PyUnaryTask.html)- Task
- Convenience alias for the common one-input, one-output case.

# cu_ahrs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cu-ahrs/1.0.0/cu_ahrs/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cu-ahrs)cu-ahrs

`cu-ahrs` is a Copper task that runs the [ uf-ahrs](https://crates.io/crates/uf-ahrs) Mahony filter on standardized IMU payloads (with optional magnetometer) to output roll, pitch, and yaw in radians.

[§](https://docs.rs#axis-convention)Axis convention

- Body frame matches the aerospace/NED convention: **+X forward**,**+Y right**,**+Z down**.
- Positive rotations follow the right-hand rule about each axis:
- Roll: right wing down is positive (rotation about +X).
- Pitch: nose up is positive (rotation about +Y).
- Yaw: clockwise when looking down along +Z (turning right) is positive.

- Accelerometer readings are expected to include gravity (a level IMU yields roughly `[0, 0, +9.81]`m/s²).

The task outputs absolute filter orientation (no startup zero reference).

[§](https://docs.rs#bare-metal-rp2350-demos)Bare-metal RP2350 demos

Two RP2350 no-std options mirroring `mpu9250-whoami`:

- `examples/rp2350_ahrs.rs`: stand-alone loop (no Copper runtime) printing RPY.
- `examples/rp2350_copper.rs`+- `examples/rp_copperconfig.ron`: full Copper app wiring- `resources::RpMpu9250Source -> cu_ahrs::CuAhrs -> tasks::RpySink`, with SPI/CS/delay provided by a normal Copper resource bundle and a dummy magnetometer source feeding the optional mag input.

```
# Host clippy/tests remain on the default host target.
cargo clippy -p cu-ahrs
cargo test -p cu-ahrs
# RP2350 firmware builds (no_std): opt-in config/target.
CARGO_CONFIG=.cargo/config.rp2350.toml cargo run --no-default-features --features rp2350-demo --example rp2350_copper
```
The RP2350 build uses `thumbv8m.main-none-eabihf` and `memory.x` matching the original `mpu9250-whoami` app. It prints RPY (radians) over RTT/defmt. Wire your MPU9250 to SPI1 pins (SCK=GPIO10, MOSI=GPIO11, MISO=GPIO12, CS=GPIO13) on Pico 2W-class boards and flash with `probe-rs`.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [sinks](https://docs.rs/sinks/index.html)
- Simple sinks for AHRS outputs.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ahrs](https://docs.rs/struct.AhrsPose.html)- Pose
- Pose expressed as Euler angles (radians) using the aerospace body frame.
- [CuAhrs](https://docs.rs/struct.CuAhrs.html)
- Copper AHRS task that fuses IMU (and optional magnetometer) payloads into roll/pitch/yaw.
- [CuAhrs](https://docs.rs/struct.CuAhrsDebugState.html)- Debug - State
- Typed debug-state view for AHRS internals.

---

# cu_aligner - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cu-aligner/1.0.0/cu_aligner/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#aligner-to-buffer-and-align-data-flow-from-different-time-horizons)Aligner to buffer and align data flow from different time horizons

The goal of this Copper component is to align data from different sources.

[§](https://docs.rs#theory-of-operation)Theory of operation:

```
        STREAM 1                STREAM 2
           │                       │
  Msg1_S1 ─╯                       │ (discarded)
           │                       │
═══════════╪═══════════════════════╪═══════════ TIME HORIZON ( present - stale_data_horizon_ms )
           │                       │
           │                       │
           │              Msg1_S2 ─┤
  Msg2_S1 ─┤                       │
           │                       │
  Msg3_S1 ─┤              Msg2_S2 ─┤
           │                       │
           │                       │
           │                       │
═══════════╪═══════════════════════╪═══════════ BEGINNING OF ALIGNMENT WINDOW ( t - alignment_window_ms )
           │                       │
           │              Msg3_S2 ─┤
  Msg4_S1 ─┤                       │           <- This part will be in the output at each process call
           │                       │
  Msg5_S1 ─┤              Msg4_S2 ─┤
           │                       │
═══════════╪═══════════════════════╪═══════════ MOST RECENT ALIGNED MESSAGE ( t )
           │                       │
           │              Msg5_S2 ─┤
           │                       │
           │              Msg6_S2 ─┤ (not yet aligned)
```
The timings are taken from the CuMsg::tov field (time of validity).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The task is generated entirely out of the `cu_aligner::define_task` macro:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use cu_aligner::define_task;
use cu29::input_msg;
use cu29::output_msg;
use cu29::cutask::Freezable;
use cu29::config::ComponentConfig;
use cu29::CuResult;
use cu29::cutask::CuTask;
use cu29::cutask::CuMsg;
// Defines a task that aligns two streams of messages, one with payloads f32, the other MyPayload (you can use any rust struct that to implement the traits for CuMsgPayload).
define_task!(MyAlignerTask,
             0 => { 15, 7, f32 },  // 15 is the Maximum capacity in nb of messages the internal
                                   // buffer structure can hold before they will me discarded,
                                   // 7 is the Maximum size in nb of messages the output (aligned messages of this type)
             1 => { 20, 5, u64 }   // or any CuMsgPayload
            // you can continue with 2 => etc...
            );
```
You defined task will need to be connected with the matching tasks upstream in the Copper config file.
The type of the input will be a tuple of CuMsg (which is what the aligner expects). From the example:
`(CuMsg<f32>, CuMsg<MyPayload>)`.
The type of the output will be a CuMsg of a tuple of CuArrays holding the aligned messages for each stream. From the
example: `CuMsg<(CuArray<f32, 7>, CuArray<MyPayload, 5>)>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#performance-consideration)Performance consideration

Copper by itself never buffers anything to avoid copies but for this aligner has to copy data until it can align it. It means you will have 1 copy from the input to the internal buffer and 1 copy from the internal buffer to the output.

If your usecase is just to get the latest message from 2 sources, just connect your task to the upstream tasks but do not use this aligner. It is only useful if the time of arrival from the 2 upstream tasks are too far apart in terms of tov.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [alignment_](https://docs.rs/macro.alignment_buffers.html)- buffers
- [define_](https://docs.rs/macro.define_task.html)- task
- Define a task that aligns incoming messages based on their timestamps See module doc for use.

# re_viewer_mcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/re_viewer_mcp/0.34.0-rc.4/re_viewer_mcp/

## Expand description

`re_viewer_mcp` — an MCP server that drives the Rerun viewer.

It reuses the full `egui_mcp` UI tool set (`query_tree`, `screenshot`, `click`, …) but, instead of
dialing a local inspection socket, it drives the viewer over rerun’s gRPC `ViewerControlService`.

Each egui tool call becomes one `egui_inspection` request/response exchange, carried by a single
`Inspect` RPC.

The server is exposed two ways — the standalone `re-viewer-mcp` binary and the `rerun viewer-mcp`
CLI subcommand.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [serve](https://docs.rs/fn.serve.html)
- Serve the MCP server over stdio until the client disconnects.

# scale-decode 0.16.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/scale-decode/0.16.2

# scale-decode

This crate makes it easy to decode SCALE encoded bytes into a custom data structure with the help of a `TypeResolver` (one of which
is a `scale_info::PortableRegistry`). By using this type information to guide decoding (instead of just trying to decode bytes based
on the shape of the target type), it's possible to be much more flexible in how data is decoded and mapped to some target type.

The main trait used to decode types is a `Visitor` trait (example below). By implementing this trait, you can describe how to
take SCALE decoded values and map them to some custom type of your choosing (whether it is a dynamically shaped type or some
static type you'd like to decode into). Implementations of this `Visitor` trait exist for many existing Rust types in the standard
library.

There also exists an `IntoVisitor` trait, which is implemented on many existing rust types and maps a given type to some visitor
implementation capable of decoding into it.

Finally, a wrapper trait, `DecodeAsType`, is auto-implemented for all types that have an `IntoVisitor` implementation,
and whose visitor errors can be turned into a standard `crate::Error`.

For custom structs and enums, one can use the `DecodeAsType` derive macro to have a `DecodeAsType` implementation automatically
generated.

Here's an example of implementing `Visitor` to decode bytes into a custom `Value` type:

```
use PhantomData;
use TypeResolver;
use ;
// A custom type we'd like to decode into:
// Implement the `Visitor` trait to define how to go from SCALE
// values into this type. Here, we are choosing to be generic over
// how types are resolved, which is a good default choice when creating
// a visitor unless you rely on a specific type resolver/ID type.
;
```
This can then be passed to a decode function like so:

```
let value: Value = decode_with_visitor?;
```
Where `scale_bytes` are the bytes you'd like to decode, `type_id` is the type stored in the `types` registry
that you'd like to try and decode the bytes into, and `types` is a `scale_type_resolver::TypeResolver` containing
information about the various types in use (a concrete implementation of this is `scale_info::PortableRegistry`).

If we were to then write an `IntoVisitor` implementation like so:

```
```
We can then also decode via tha automatic `DecodeAsType` impl like so:

```
use DecodeAsType;
let value = decode_as_type?;
```
With an `IntoVisitor` impl, you'd also benefit from being able to decode things like `Vec<Value>`,
`(Value, bool)`, `Arc<Value>` and so on in the same way.

---

                    scale-decode 0.16.2

                Decode SCALE encoded bytes into arbitrary types at runtime

# scale_decode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/scale-decode/0.16.2/target-redirect/scale_decode/

## Expand description

`parity-scale-codec` provides a `Decode` trait which allows bytes to be scale decoded into types based on the shape of those
types. This crate builds on this, and allows bytes to be decoded into types based on type information, rather than the shape
of the target type. At a high level, this crate just aims to do the reverse of the `scale-encode` crate.

This crate exposes four traits:

- A `visitor::Visitor``visitor::decode_with_visitor`
- An `IntoVisitor``visitor::Visitor`
- A `DecodeAsType``IntoVisitor``scale_type_resolver::TypeResolver`
- A `DecodeAsFields``Field`

Implementations for many built-in types are also provided for each trait, and the [ DecodeAsType](https://docs.rs/derive.DecodeAsType.html) macro can be used to
generate the relevant impls on new struct and enum types such that they get a

[impl.](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsType.html)

`DecodeAsType`The [ DecodeAsType](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsType.html) and

[traits are basically the mirror of](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsFields.html)

`DecodeAsFields``scale-encode`’s `EncodeAsType` and `EncodeAsFields`
traits in terms of their interface.[§](https://docs.rs#motivation)Motivation

By de-coupling the shape of a type from how bytes are decoded into it, we make it much more likely that the decoding will succeed, and are no longer reliant on types having a precise layout in order to be decoded into correctly. Some examples of this follow.

```
use codec::Encode;
use scale_decode::DecodeAsType;
use scale_info::{PortableRegistry, TypeInfo};
use std::fmt::Debug;
// We normally expect to have type information to hand, but for our examples
// we construct type info from any type that implements `TypeInfo`.
fn get_type_info<T: TypeInfo + 'static>() -> (u32, PortableRegistry) {
    let m = scale_info::MetaType::new::<T>();
    let mut types = scale_info::Registry::new();
    let ty = types.register_type(&m);
    let portable_registry: PortableRegistry = types.into();
    (ty.id, portable_registry)
}
// Encode the left value statically.
// Decode those bytes into the right type via `DecodeAsType`.
// Assert that the decoded bytes are identical to the right value.
fn assert_decodes_to<A, B>(a: A, b: B)
where
    A: Encode + TypeInfo + 'static,
    B: DecodeAsType + PartialEq + Debug,
{
    let (type_id, types) = get_type_info::<A>();
    let a_bytes = a.encode();
    let new_b = B::decode_as_type(&mut &*a_bytes, type_id, &types).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(b, new_b);
}
// Start simple; a u8 can DecodeAsType into a u64 and vice versa. Numbers will all
// try to convert into the desired output size, failing if this isn't possible:
assert_decodes_to(123u64, 123u8);
assert_decodes_to(123u8, 123u64);
// Compact decoding is also handled "under the hood" by DecodeAsType, so no "compact"
// annotations are needed on values.
assert_decodes_to(codec::Compact(123u64), 123u64);
// Enum variants are lined up by variant name, so no explicit "index" annotation are
// needed either; DecodeAsType will take care of it.
#[derive(Encode, TypeInfo)]
enum Foo {
    #[codec(index = 10)]
    Something(u64),
}
#[derive(DecodeAsType, PartialEq, Debug)]
enum FooTarget {
    Something(u128),
}
assert_decodes_to(Foo::Something(123), FooTarget::Something(123));
// DecodeAsType will skip annotated fields and not look for them in the encoded bytes.
// #[codec(skip)] and #[decode_as_type(skip)] both work.
#[derive(Encode, TypeInfo)]
struct Bar {
    a: bool,
}
#[derive(DecodeAsType, PartialEq, Debug)]
struct BarTarget {
    a: bool,
    #[decode_as_type(skip)]
    b: String,
}
assert_decodes_to(
    Bar { a: true },
    BarTarget { a: true, b: String::new() },
);
// DecodeAsType impls will generally skip through any newtype wrappers.
#[derive(DecodeAsType, Encode, TypeInfo, PartialEq, Debug)]
struct Wrapper {
    value: u64
}
assert_decodes_to(
    (Wrapper { value: 123 },),
    123u64
);
assert_decodes_to(
    123u64,
    (123,)
);
// Things like arrays and sequences are generally interchangeable despite the
// encoding format being slightly different:
assert_decodes_to([1u8,2,3,4,5], vec![1u64,2,3,4,5]);
assert_decodes_to(vec![1u64,2,3,4,5], [1u8,2,3,4,5]);
```
If this high level interface isn’t suitable, you can implement your own [ visitor::Visitor](https://docs.rs/visitor/trait.Visitor.html)’s. These can support zero-copy decoding
(unlike the higher level

[interface), and generally the Visitor construction and execution is zero alloc, allowing for efficient type based decoding.](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsType.html)

`DecodeAsType`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- An error that is emitted whenever some decoding fails.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Re-exports of external crates.
- [visitor](https://docs.rs/visitor/index.html)
- The `Visitor`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.Field.html)
- Information about a composite field.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsFields.html)- AsFields
- This is similar to `DecodeAsType``DecodeAsType`
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsType.html)- AsType
- This trait is implemented for any type `T`where`T`implements`IntoVisitor``Visitor``Error``visitor::decode_with_visitor``scale-encode`’s`EncodeAsType`.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/trait.FieldIter.html)- Iter
- An iterator over a set of fields.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoVisitor.html)- Visitor
- This trait can be implemented on any type that has an associated `Visitor``Error``DecodeAsType`
- [Type](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html)- Resolver
- This trait can be implemented for any type that is capable of describing how some type (identified
by a `TypeResolver::TypeId`

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Decode](https://docs.rs/derive.DecodeAsType.html)- AsType
- The `DecodeAsType`derive macro can be used to implement`DecodeAsType`on structs and enums whose fields all implement`DecodeAsType`. Under the hood, the macro generates`scale_decode::visitor::Visitor`and`scale_decode::IntoVisitor`implementations for each type (as well as an associated`Visitor`struct), which in turn means that the type will automatically implement`scale_decode::DecodeAsType`.

# List of all items

# scale_decode/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)// Copyright (C) 2023 Parity Technologies (UK) Ltd. (admin@parity.io)
[2](https://docs.rs#2)// This file is a part of the scale-decode crate.
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//
[4](https://docs.rs#4)// Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 (the "License");
[5](https://docs.rs#5)// you may not use this file except in compliance with the License.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)// You may obtain a copy of the License at
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//         http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//
[10](https://docs.rs#10)// Unless required by applicable law or agreed to in writing, software
[11](https://docs.rs#11)// distributed under the License is distributed on an "AS IS" BASIS,
[12](https://docs.rs#12)// WITHOUT WARRANTIES OR CONDITIONS OF ANY KIND, either express or implied.
[13](https://docs.rs#13)// See the License for the specific language governing permissions and
[14](https://docs.rs#14)// limitations under the License.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)
[16](https://docs.rs#16)#![no_std]
[17](https://docs.rs#17)
[18](https://docs.rs#18)/*!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)`parity-scale-codec` provides a `Decode` trait which allows bytes to be scale decoded into types based on the shape of those
[20](https://docs.rs#20)types. This crate builds on this, and allows bytes to be decoded into types based on type information, rather than the shape
[21](https://docs.rs#21)of the target type. At a high level, this crate just aims to do the reverse of the `scale-encode` crate.
[22](https://docs.rs#22)
[23](https://docs.rs#23)This crate exposes four traits:
[24](https://docs.rs#24)
[25](https://docs.rs#25)- A [`visitor::Visitor`] trait which when implemented on some type, can be used in conjunction with [`visitor::decode_with_visitor`]
[26](https://docs.rs#26)  to decode SCALE encoded bytes based on some type information into some arbitrary type.
[27](https://docs.rs#27)- An [`IntoVisitor`] trait which can be used to obtain the [`visitor::Visitor`] implementation for some type.
[28](https://docs.rs#28)- A [`DecodeAsType`] trait which is implemented for types which implement [`IntoVisitor`], and provides a high level interface for
[29](https://docs.rs#29)  decoding SCALE encoded bytes into some type with the help of a type ID and a [`scale_type_resolver::TypeResolver`].
[30](https://docs.rs#30)- A [`DecodeAsFields`] trait which when implemented on some type, describes how SCALE encoded bytes can be decoded
[31](https://docs.rs#31)  into it with the help of an iterator of [`Field`]s and a type registry describing the shape of the encoded bytes. This is
[32](https://docs.rs#32)  generally only implemented for tuples and structs, since we need a set of fields to map to the provided slices.
[33](https://docs.rs#33)
[34](https://docs.rs#34)Implementations for many built-in types are also provided for each trait, and the [`macro@DecodeAsType`] macro can be used to
[35](https://docs.rs#35)generate the relevant impls on new struct and enum types such that they get a [`DecodeAsType`] impl.
[36](https://docs.rs#36)
[37](https://docs.rs#37)The [`DecodeAsType`] and [`DecodeAsFields`] traits are basically the mirror of `scale-encode`'s `EncodeAsType` and `EncodeAsFields`
[38](https://docs.rs#38)traits in terms of their interface.
[39](https://docs.rs#39)
[40](https://docs.rs#40)# Motivation
[41](https://docs.rs#41)
[42](https://docs.rs#42)By de-coupling the shape of a type from how bytes are decoded into it, we make it much more likely that the decoding will succeed,
[43](https://docs.rs#43)and are no longer reliant on types having a precise layout in order to be decoded into correctly. Some examples of this follow.
[44](https://docs.rs#44)
[45](https://docs.rs#45)```rust
[46](https://docs.rs#46)use codec::Encode;
[47](https://docs.rs#47)use scale_decode::DecodeAsType;
[48](https://docs.rs#48)use scale_info::{PortableRegistry, TypeInfo};
[49](https://docs.rs#49)use std::fmt::Debug;
[50](https://docs.rs#50)
[51](https://docs.rs#51)// We normally expect to have type information to hand, but for our examples
[52](https://docs.rs#52)// we construct type info from any type that implements `TypeInfo`.
[53](https://docs.rs#53)fn get_type_info<T: TypeInfo + 'static>() -> (u32, PortableRegistry) {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)    let m = scale_info::MetaType::new::<T>();
[55](https://docs.rs#55)    let mut types = scale_info::Registry::new();
[56](https://docs.rs#56)    let ty = types.register_type(&m);
[57](https://docs.rs#57)    let portable_registry: PortableRegistry = types.into();
[58](https://docs.rs#58)    (ty.id, portable_registry)
[59](https://docs.rs#59)}
[60](https://docs.rs#60)
[61](https://docs.rs#61)// Encode the left value statically.
[62](https://docs.rs#62)// Decode those bytes into the right type via `DecodeAsType`.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)// Assert that the decoded bytes are identical to the right value.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)fn assert_decodes_to<A, B>(a: A, b: B)
[65](https://docs.rs#65)where
[66](https://docs.rs#66)    A: Encode + TypeInfo + 'static,
[67](https://docs.rs#67)    B: DecodeAsType + PartialEq + Debug,
[68](https://docs.rs#68){
[69](https://docs.rs#69)    let (type_id, types) = get_type_info::<A>();
[70](https://docs.rs#70)    let a_bytes = a.encode();
[71](https://docs.rs#71)    let new_b = B::decode_as_type(&mut &*a_bytes, type_id, &types).unwrap();
[72](https://docs.rs#72)    assert_eq!(b, new_b);
[73](https://docs.rs#73)}
[74](https://docs.rs#74)
[75](https://docs.rs#75)// Start simple; a u8 can DecodeAsType into a u64 and vice versa. Numbers will all
[76](https://docs.rs#76)// try to convert into the desired output size, failing if this isn't possible:
[77](https://docs.rs#77)assert_decodes_to(123u64, 123u8);
[78](https://docs.rs#78)assert_decodes_to(123u8, 123u64);
[79](https://docs.rs#79)
[80](https://docs.rs#80)// Compact decoding is also handled "under the hood" by DecodeAsType, so no "compact"
[81](https://docs.rs#81)// annotations are needed on values.
[82](https://docs.rs#82)assert_decodes_to(codec::Compact(123u64), 123u64);
[83](https://docs.rs#83)
[84](https://docs.rs#84)// Enum variants are lined up by variant name, so no explicit "index" annotation are
[85](https://docs.rs#85)// needed either; DecodeAsType will take care of it.
[86](https://docs.rs#86)#[derive(Encode, TypeInfo)]
[87](https://docs.rs#87)enum Foo {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)    #[codec(index = 10)]
[89](https://docs.rs#89)    Something(u64),
[90](https://docs.rs#90)}
[91](https://docs.rs#91)#[derive(DecodeAsType, PartialEq, Debug)]
[92](https://docs.rs#92)enum FooTarget {
[93](https://docs.rs#93)    Something(u128),
[94](https://docs.rs#94)}
[95](https://docs.rs#95)assert_decodes_to(Foo::Something(123), FooTarget::Something(123));
[96](https://docs.rs#96)
[97](https://docs.rs#97)// DecodeAsType will skip annotated fields and not look for them in the encoded bytes.
[98](https://docs.rs#98)// #[codec(skip)] and #[decode_as_type(skip)] both work.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)#[derive(Encode, TypeInfo)]
[100](https://docs.rs#100)struct Bar {
[101](https://docs.rs#101)    a: bool,
[102](https://docs.rs#102)}
[103](https://docs.rs#103)#[derive(DecodeAsType, PartialEq, Debug)]
[104](https://docs.rs#104)struct BarTarget {
[105](https://docs.rs#105)    a: bool,
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    #[decode_as_type(skip)]
[107](https://docs.rs#107)    b: String,
[108](https://docs.rs#108)}
[109](https://docs.rs#109)assert_decodes_to(
[110](https://docs.rs#110)    Bar { a: true },
[111](https://docs.rs#111)    BarTarget { a: true, b: String::new() },
[112](https://docs.rs#112));
[113](https://docs.rs#113)
[114](https://docs.rs#114)// DecodeAsType impls will generally skip through any newtype wrappers.
[115](https://docs.rs#115)#[derive(DecodeAsType, Encode, TypeInfo, PartialEq, Debug)]
[116](https://docs.rs#116)struct Wrapper {
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    value: u64
[118](https://docs.rs#118)}
[119](https://docs.rs#119)assert_decodes_to(
[120](https://docs.rs#120)    (Wrapper { value: 123 },),
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    123u64
[122](https://docs.rs#122));
[123](https://docs.rs#123)assert_decodes_to(
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    123u64,
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    (123,)
[126](https://docs.rs#126));
[127](https://docs.rs#127)
[128](https://docs.rs#128)// Things like arrays and sequences are generally interchangeable despite the
[129](https://docs.rs#129)// encoding format being slightly different:
[130](https://docs.rs#130)assert_decodes_to([1u8,2,3,4,5], vec![1u64,2,3,4,5]);
[131](https://docs.rs#131)assert_decodes_to(vec![1u64,2,3,4,5], [1u8,2,3,4,5]);
[132](https://docs.rs#132)```
[133](https://docs.rs#133)
[134](https://docs.rs#134)If this high level interface isn't suitable, you can implement your own [`visitor::Visitor`]'s. These can support zero-copy decoding
[135](https://docs.rs#135)(unlike the higher level [`DecodeAsType`] interface), and generally the Visitor construction and execution is zero alloc, allowing
[136](https://docs.rs#136)for efficient type based decoding.
[137](https://docs.rs#137)*/
[138](https://docs.rs#138)#![deny(missing_docs)]
[139](https://docs.rs#139)
[140](https://docs.rs#140)extern crate alloc;
[141](https://docs.rs#141)
[142](https://docs.rs#142)mod impls;
[143](https://docs.rs#143)
[144](https://docs.rs#144)pub mod error;
[145](https://docs.rs#145)pub mod visitor;
[146](https://docs.rs#146)
[147](https://docs.rs#147)pub use crate::error::Error;
[148](https://docs.rs#148)pub use scale_type_resolver::Field;
[149](https://docs.rs#149)pub use scale_type_resolver::FieldIter;
[150](https://docs.rs#150)pub use scale_type_resolver::TypeResolver;
[151](https://docs.rs#151)pub use visitor::Visitor;
[152](https://docs.rs#152)
[153](https://docs.rs#153)// This is exported for generated derive code to use, to be compatible with std or no-std as needed.
[154](https://docs.rs#154)#[doc(hidden)]
[155](https://docs.rs#155)pub use alloc::{collections::BTreeMap, string::ToString, vec};
[156](https://docs.rs#156)
[157](https://docs.rs#157)/// Re-exports of external crates.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)pub mod ext {
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    #[cfg(feature = "primitive-types")]
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    pub use primitive_types;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    pub use scale_type_resolver;
[162](https://docs.rs#162)}
[163](https://docs.rs#163)
[164](https://docs.rs#164)/// This trait is implemented for any type `T` where `T` implements [`IntoVisitor`] and the errors returned
[165](https://docs.rs#165)/// from this [`Visitor`] can be converted into [`Error`]. It's essentially a convenience wrapper around
[166](https://docs.rs#166)/// [`visitor::decode_with_visitor`] that mirrors `scale-encode`'s `EncodeAsType`.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)pub trait DecodeAsType: Sized + IntoVisitor {
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    /// Given some input bytes, a `type_id`, and type registry, attempt to decode said bytes into
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    /// `Self`. Implementations should modify the `&mut` reference to the bytes such that any bytes
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// not used in the course of decoding are still pointed to after decoding is complete.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    fn decode_as_type<R: TypeResolver>(
[172](https://docs.rs#172)        input: &mut &[u8],
[173](https://docs.rs#173)        type_id: R::TypeId,
[174](https://docs.rs#174)        types: &R,
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    ) -> Result<Self, Error> {
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        Self::decode_as_type_maybe_compact(input, type_id, types, false)
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    }
[178](https://docs.rs#178)
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// Given some input bytes, a `type_id`, and type registry, attempt to decode said bytes into
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// `Self`. Implementations should modify the `&mut` reference to the bytes such that any bytes
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    /// not used in the course of decoding are still pointed to after decoding is complete.
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    ///
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// If is_compact=true, it is assumed the value is compact encoded (only works for some types).
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    #[doc(hidden)]
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    fn decode_as_type_maybe_compact<R: TypeResolver>(
[186](https://docs.rs#186)        input: &mut &[u8],
[187](https://docs.rs#187)        type_id: R::TypeId,
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        types: &R,
[189](https://docs.rs#189)        is_compact: bool,
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    ) -> Result<Self, Error>;
[191](https://docs.rs#191)}
[192](https://docs.rs#192)
[193](https://docs.rs#193)impl<T: Sized + IntoVisitor> DecodeAsType for T {
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    fn decode_as_type_maybe_compact<R: TypeResolver>(
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        input: &mut &[u8],
[196](https://docs.rs#196)        type_id: R::TypeId,
[197](https://docs.rs#197)        types: &R,
[198](https://docs.rs#198)        is_compact: bool,
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    ) -> Result<Self, Error> {
[200](https://docs.rs#200)        let res = visitor::decode_with_visitor_maybe_compact(
[201](https://docs.rs#201)            input,
[202](https://docs.rs#202)            type_id,
[203](https://docs.rs#203)            types,
[204](https://docs.rs#204)            T::into_visitor::<R>(),
[205](https://docs.rs#205)            is_compact,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)        )?;
[207](https://docs.rs#207)        Ok(res)
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    }
[209](https://docs.rs#209)}
[210](https://docs.rs#210)
[211](https://docs.rs#211)/// This is similar to [`DecodeAsType`], except that it's instead implemented for types that can be given a list of
[212](https://docs.rs#212)/// fields denoting the type being decoded from and attempt to do this decoding. This is generally implemented just
[213](https://docs.rs#213)/// for tuple and struct types, and is automatically implemented via the [`macro@DecodeAsType`] macro.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)pub trait DecodeAsFields: Sized {
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    /// Given some bytes and some fields denoting their structure, attempt to decode.
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    fn decode_as_fields<'resolver, R: TypeResolver>(
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        input: &mut &[u8],
[218](https://docs.rs#218)        fields: &mut dyn FieldIter<'resolver, R::TypeId>,
[219](https://docs.rs#219)        types: &'resolver R,
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    ) -> Result<Self, Error>;
[221](https://docs.rs#221)}
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// This trait can be implemented on any type that has an associated [`Visitor`] responsible for decoding
[224](https://docs.rs#224)/// SCALE encoded bytes to it whose error type is [`Error`]. Anything that implements this trait gets a
[225](https://docs.rs#225)/// [`DecodeAsType`] implementation for free.
[226](https://docs.rs#226)// Dev note: This used to allow for any Error type that could be converted into `scale_decode::Error`.
[227](https://docs.rs#227)// The problem with this is that the `DecodeAsType` trait became tricky to use in some contexts, because it
[228](https://docs.rs#228)// didn't automatically imply so much. Realistically, being stricter here shouldn't matter too much; derive
[229](https://docs.rs#229)// impls all use `scale_decode::Error` anyway, and manual impls can just manually convert into the error
[230](https://docs.rs#230)// rather than rely on auto conversion, if they care about also being able to impl `DecodeAsType`.
[231](https://docs.rs#231)pub trait IntoVisitor {
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// The visitor type used to decode SCALE encoded bytes to `Self`.
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    type AnyVisitor<R: TypeResolver>: for<'scale, 'resolver> visitor::Visitor<
[234](https://docs.rs#234)        Value<'scale, 'resolver> = Self,
[235](https://docs.rs#235)        Error = Error,
[236](https://docs.rs#236)        TypeResolver = R,
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    >;
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    /// A means of obtaining this visitor.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    fn into_visitor<R: TypeResolver>() -> Self::AnyVisitor<R>;
[240](https://docs.rs#240)}
[241](https://docs.rs#241)
[242](https://docs.rs#242)/// The `DecodeAsType` derive macro can be used to implement `DecodeAsType` on structs and enums whose
[243](https://docs.rs#243)/// fields all implement `DecodeAsType`. Under the hood, the macro generates `scale_decode::visitor::Visitor`
[244](https://docs.rs#244)/// and `scale_decode::IntoVisitor` implementations for each type (as well as an associated `Visitor` struct),
[245](https://docs.rs#245)/// which in turn means that the type will automatically implement `scale_decode::DecodeAsType`.
[246](https://docs.rs#246)///
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// # Examples
[248](https://docs.rs#248)///
[249](https://docs.rs#249)/// This can be applied to structs and enums:
[250](https://docs.rs#250)///
[251](https://docs.rs#251)/// ```rust
[252](https://docs.rs#252)/// use scale_decode::DecodeAsType;
[253](https://docs.rs#253)///
[254](https://docs.rs#254)/// #[derive(DecodeAsType)]
[255](https://docs.rs#255)/// struct Foo(String);
[256](https://docs.rs#256)///
[257](https://docs.rs#257)/// #[derive(DecodeAsType)]
[258](https://docs.rs#258)/// struct Bar {
[259](https://docs.rs#259)///     a: u64,
[260](https://docs.rs#260)///     b: bool
[261](https://docs.rs#261)/// }
[262](https://docs.rs#262)///
[263](https://docs.rs#263)/// #[derive(DecodeAsType)]
[264](https://docs.rs#264)/// enum Wibble<T> {
[265](https://docs.rs#265)///     A(usize, bool, T),
[266](https://docs.rs#266)///     B { value: String },
[267](https://docs.rs#267)///     C
[268](https://docs.rs#268)/// }
[269](https://docs.rs#269)/// ```
[270](https://docs.rs#270)///
[271](https://docs.rs#271)/// If you aren't directly depending on `scale_decode`, you must tell the macro what the path
[272](https://docs.rs#272)/// to it is so that it knows how to generate the relevant impls:
[273](https://docs.rs#273)///
[274](https://docs.rs#274)/// ```rust
[275](https://docs.rs#275)/// # use scale_decode as alt_path;
[276](https://docs.rs#276)/// use alt_path::DecodeAsType;
[277](https://docs.rs#277)///
[278](https://docs.rs#278)/// #[derive(DecodeAsType)]
[279](https://docs.rs#279)/// #[decode_as_type(crate_path = "alt_path")]
[280](https://docs.rs#280)/// struct Foo<T> {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)///    a: u64,
[282](https://docs.rs#282)///    b: T
[283](https://docs.rs#283)/// }
[284](https://docs.rs#284)/// ```
[285](https://docs.rs#285)///
[286](https://docs.rs#286)/// If you use generics, the macro will assume that each of them also implements `EncodeAsType`.
[287](https://docs.rs#287)/// This can be overridden when it's not the case (the compiler will ensure that you can't go wrong here):
[288](https://docs.rs#288)///
[289](https://docs.rs#289)/// ```rust
[290](https://docs.rs#290)/// use scale_decode::DecodeAsType;
[291](https://docs.rs#291)///
[292](https://docs.rs#292)/// #[derive(DecodeAsType)]
[293](https://docs.rs#293)/// #[decode_as_type(trait_bounds = "")]
[294](https://docs.rs#294)/// struct Foo<T> {
[295](https://docs.rs#295)///    a: u64,
[296](https://docs.rs#296)///    b: bool,
[297](https://docs.rs#297)///    #[decode_as_type(skip)]
[298](https://docs.rs#298)///    c: std::marker::PhantomData<T>
[299](https://docs.rs#299)/// }
[300](https://docs.rs#300)/// ```
[301](https://docs.rs#301)///
[302](https://docs.rs#302)/// You'll note that we can also opt to skip fields that we don't want to decode into; such fields will receive
[303](https://docs.rs#303)/// their default value and no attempt to decode SCALE bytes into them will occur.
[304](https://docs.rs#304)///
[305](https://docs.rs#305)/// # Attributes
[306](https://docs.rs#306)///
[307](https://docs.rs#307)/// - `#[decode_as_type(crate_path = "::path::to::scale_decode")]`:
[308](https://docs.rs#308)///   By default, the macro expects `scale_decode` to be a top level dependency,
[309](https://docs.rs#309)///   available as `::scale_decode`. If this is not the case, you can provide the
[310](https://docs.rs#310)///   crate path here.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)/// - `#[decode_as_type(trait_bounds = "T: Foo, U::Input: DecodeAsType")]`:
[312](https://docs.rs#312)///   By default, for each generate type parameter, the macro will add trait bounds such
[313](https://docs.rs#313)///   that these type parameters must implement `DecodeAsType` too. You can override this
[314](https://docs.rs#314)///   behaviour and provide your own trait bounds instead using this option.
[315](https://docs.rs#315)/// - `#[decode_as_type(skip)]` (or `#[codec(skip)]`):
[316](https://docs.rs#316)///   Any fields annotated with this will be skipped when attempting to decode into the
[317](https://docs.rs#317)///   type, and instead will be populated with their default value (and therefore must
[318](https://docs.rs#318)///   implement [`core::default::Default`]).
[319](https://docs.rs#319)#[cfg(feature = "derive")]
[320](https://docs.rs#320)pub use scale_decode_derive::DecodeAsType;

---

}## Expand description

An implementation of the [ Visitor](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html) trait can be passed to the

[function, and is handed back values as they are encountered. It’s up to the implementation to decide what to do with these values.](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_with_visitor.html)

`decode_with_visitor()`## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/scale_decode/visitor/mod.rs.html#54-61)#### fn [unchecked_decode_as_type](https://docs.rs#method.unchecked_decode_as_type)<'scale, 'resolver>(
    self,
    _input: &mut &'scale [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)],
    _type_id: [TypeIdFor](https://docs.rs/type.TypeIdFor.html)<Self>,
    _types: &'resolver Self::[TypeResolver](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html#associatedtype.TypeResolver),
) -> [DecodeAsTypeResult](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeAsTypeResult.html)<Self, [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[Value](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html#associatedtype.Value)<'scale, 'resolver>, Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html#associatedtype.Error)>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/scale_decode/visitor/mod.rs.html#54-61)

#### fn [unchecked_decode_as_type](https://docs.rs#method.unchecked_decode_as_type)<'scale, 'resolver>(
    self,
    _input: &mut &'scale [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)],
    _type_id: [TypeIdFor](https://docs.rs/type.TypeIdFor.html)<Self>,
    _types: &'resolver Self::[TypeResolver](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html#associatedtype.TypeResolver),
) -> [DecodeAsTypeResult](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeAsTypeResult.html)<Self, [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[Value](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html#associatedtype.Value)<'scale, 'resolver>, Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html#associatedtype.Error)>>

This method is called immediately upon running [ decode_with_visitor()](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_with_visitor.html). By default we ignore
this call and return our visitor back (ie

[). If you choose to do some decoding at this stage, return](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeAsTypeResult.html#variant.Skipped)

`DecodeAsTypeResult::Skipped`[. In either case, any bytes that you consume from the input (by altering what it points to) will be consumed for any subsequent visiting.](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeAsTypeResult.html#variant.Decoded)

`DecodeAsTypeResult::Decoded`[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

Unlike the other `visit_*` methods, it is completely up to the implementor to decode and advance the
bytes in a sensible way, and thus also possible for the implementor to screw this up. As a result,
it’s suggested that you don’t implement this unless you know what you’re doing.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/scale_decode/visitor/mod.rs.html#66-71)#### fn [visit_unexpected](https://docs.rs#method.visit_unexpected)<'scale, 'resolver>(
    self,

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/scale_decode/visitor/mod.rs.html#66-71)

#### fn [visit_unexpected](https://docs.rs#method.visit_unexpected)<'scale, 'resolver>(
    self,
    unexpected: [Unexpected](https://docs.rs/enum.Unexpected.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[Value](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html#associatedtype.Value)<'scale, 'resolver>, Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html#associatedtype.Error)>

This is called when a visitor function that you’ve not provided an implementation is called. You are provided an enum value corresponding to the function call, and can decide what to return in this case. The default is to return an error to announce the unexpected value.

# decode_with_visitor in scale_decode::visitor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/scale-decode/0.16.2/scale_decode/visitor/fn.decode_with_visitor.html

`pub fn decode_with_visitor<'scale, 'resolver, V: `[Visitor](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html)>(
    data: &mut &'scale [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)],
    ty_id: [TypeIdFor](https://docs.rs/type.TypeIdFor.html)<V>,
    types: &'resolver V::[TypeResolver](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html#associatedtype.TypeResolver),
    visitor: V,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<V::[Value](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html#associatedtype.Value)<'scale, 'resolver>, V::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html#associatedtype.Error)>## Expand description

Decode data according to the type ID and type resolver provided.
The provided pointer to the data slice will be moved forwards as needed
depending on what was decoded, and a method on the provided [ Visitor](https://docs.rs/trait.Visitor.html)
will be called depending on the type that needs to be decoded.

---

# IntoVisitor in scale_decode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/scale-decode/0.16.2/scale_decode/trait.IntoVisitor.html

```
pub trait IntoVisitor {
    type
```
[AnyVisitor](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.AnyVisitor)<R: [TypeResolver](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html)>: for<'scale, 'resolver> [Visitor](https://docs.rs/visitor/trait.Visitor.html)<Value<'scale, 'resolver> = Self, Error = [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html), TypeResolver = R>;
    // Required method
    fn [into_visitor](https://docs.rs#tymethod.into_visitor)<R: [TypeResolver](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html)>() -> Self::[AnyVisitor](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoVisitor.html#associatedtype.AnyVisitor)<R>;
}## Expand description

This trait can be implemented on any type that has an associated [ Visitor](https://docs.rs/visitor/trait.Visitor.html) responsible for decoding
SCALE encoded bytes to it whose error type is

[. Anything that implements this trait gets a](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)

`Error`[implementation for free.](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsType.html)

# DecodeAsType in scale_decode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/scale-decode/0.16.2/scale_decode/trait.DecodeAsType.html

`pub trait DecodeAsType: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) + [IntoVisitor](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoVisitor.html) {
    // Provided method
    fn [decode_as_type](https://docs.rs#method.decode_as_type)<R: [TypeResolver](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html)>(
        input: &mut &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)],
        type_id: R::[TypeId](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html#associatedtype.TypeId),
        types: [&R](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html),
    ) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)> { ... }
}## Expand description

This trait is implemented for any type `T` where `T` implements [ IntoVisitor](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoVisitor.html) and the errors returned
from this

[can be converted into](https://docs.rs/visitor/trait.Visitor.html)

`Visitor`[. It’s essentially a convenience wrapper around](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)

`Error`[that mirrors](https://docs.rs/visitor/fn.decode_with_visitor.html)

`visitor::decode_with_visitor``scale-encode`’s `EncodeAsType`.## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/scale_decode/lib.rs.html#171-177)#### fn [decode_as_type](https://docs.rs#method.decode_as_type)<R: [TypeResolver](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html)>(
    input: &mut &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)],
    type_id: R::[TypeId](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html#associatedtype.TypeId),
    types: [&R](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/scale_decode/lib.rs.html#171-177)

#### fn [decode_as_type](https://docs.rs#method.decode_as_type)<R: [TypeResolver](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html)>(
    input: &mut &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)],
    type_id: R::[TypeId](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html#associatedtype.TypeId),
    types: [&R](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/struct.Error.html)>

Given some input bytes, a `type_id`, and type registry, attempt to decode said bytes into
`Self`. Implementations should modify the `&mut` reference to the bytes such that any bytes
not used in the course of decoding are still pointed to after decoding is complete.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# TypeResolver in scale_decode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/scale-decode/0.16.2/scale_decode/trait.TypeResolver.html

```
pub trait TypeResolver {
    type
```
[TypeId](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.TypeId): [TypeId](https://docs.rs/scale-type-resolver/0.2.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/scale_type_resolver/trait.TypeId.html) + 'static;
    type [Error](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Error): [Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) + [Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html);
    // Required method
    fn [resolve_type](https://docs.rs#tymethod.resolve_type)<'this, V>(
        &'this self,
        type_id: Self::[TypeId](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html#associatedtype.TypeId),
        visitor: V,
    ) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<<V as [ResolvedTypeVisitor](https://docs.rs/scale-type-resolver/0.2.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/scale_type_resolver/trait.ResolvedTypeVisitor.html)<'this>>::[Value](https://docs.rs/scale-type-resolver/0.2.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/scale_type_resolver/trait.ResolvedTypeVisitor.html#associatedtype.Value), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where V: [ResolvedTypeVisitor](https://docs.rs/scale-type-resolver/0.2.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/scale_type_resolver/trait.ResolvedTypeVisitor.html)<'this, TypeId = Self::[TypeId](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html#associatedtype.TypeId)>;
}## Expand description

This trait can be implemented for any type that is capable of describing how some type (identified
by a [ TypeResolver::TypeId](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html#associatedtype.TypeId)) is represented in terms of SCALE encoded bytes.

The naive way of implementing a trait like this would be to have a function that takes in a type ID
and returns an enum which represents how the type is SCALE encoded. However, building such an enum
to describe more complex types would likely involve allocating, which we’d rather avoid where possible.
Instead, the approach taken here is to provide a set of callbacks to the [ TypeResolver::resolve_type()](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeResolver.html#tymethod.resolve_type)
via a

[implementation. Exactly one of these callbacks is fired (and provided the necessary information) depending on the outcome of resolving a given type. This allows us to be far more flexible about how we hand back the required information, which avoids allocations.](https://docs.rs/scale-type-resolver/0.2.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/scale_type_resolver/trait.ResolvedTypeVisitor.html)

`ResolvedTypeVisitor`For an example implementation, see the code in the [`portable_registry`] module.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

        types: [&'resolver R](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html),

}## Expand description

This is similar to [ DecodeAsType](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsType.html), except that it’s instead implemented for types that can be given a list of
fields denoting the type being decoded from and attempt to do this decoding. This is generally implemented just
for tuple and struct types, and is automatically implemented via the

[macro.](https://docs.rs/derive.DecodeAsType.html)

`DecodeAsType`## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

# DecodeAsType in scale_decode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/scale-decode/0.16.2/scale_decode/derive.DecodeAsType.html

```
#[derive(DecodeAsType)]
{
    // Attributes available to this derive:
    #[decode_as_type]
    #[codec]
}
```
## Expand description

The `DecodeAsType` derive macro can be used to implement `DecodeAsType` on structs and enums whose
fields all implement `DecodeAsType`. Under the hood, the macro generates `scale_decode::visitor::Visitor`
and `scale_decode::IntoVisitor` implementations for each type (as well as an associated `Visitor` struct),
which in turn means that the type will automatically implement `scale_decode::DecodeAsType`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

This can be applied to structs and enums:

```
use scale_decode::DecodeAsType;
#[derive(DecodeAsType)]
struct Foo(String);
#[derive(DecodeAsType)]
struct Bar {
    a: u64,
    b: bool
}
#[derive(DecodeAsType)]
enum Wibble<T> {
    A(usize, bool, T),
    B { value: String },
    C
}
```
If you aren’t directly depending on `scale_decode`, you must tell the macro what the path
to it is so that it knows how to generate the relevant impls:

```
use alt_path::DecodeAsType;
#[derive(DecodeAsType)]
#[decode_as_type(crate_path = "alt_path")]
struct Foo<T> {
   a: u64,
   b: T
}
```
If you use generics, the macro will assume that each of them also implements `EncodeAsType`.
This can be overridden when it’s not the case (the compiler will ensure that you can’t go wrong here):

```
use scale_decode::DecodeAsType;
#[derive(DecodeAsType)]
#[decode_as_type(trait_bounds = "")]
struct Foo<T> {
   a: u64,
   b: bool,
   #[decode_as_type(skip)]
   c: std::marker::PhantomData<T>
}
```
You’ll note that we can also opt to skip fields that we don’t want to decode into; such fields will receive their default value and no attempt to decode SCALE bytes into them will occur.

[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)Attributes

- `#[decode_as_type(crate_path = "::path::to::scale_decode")]`: By default, the macro expects- `scale_decode`to be a top level dependency, available as- `::scale_decode`. If this is not the case, you can provide the crate path here.
- `#[decode_as_type(trait_bounds = "T: Foo, U::Input: DecodeAsType")]`: By default, for each generate type parameter, the macro will add trait bounds such that these type parameters must implement- `DecodeAsType`too. You can override this behaviour and provide your own trait bounds instead using this option.
- `#[decode_as_type(skip)]`(or- `#[codec(skip)]`): Any fields annotated with this will be skipped when attempting to decode into the type, and instead will be populated with their default value (and therefore must implement- `core::default::Default`

# scale_decode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/scale-decode/latest/scale_decode/

## Expand description

`parity-scale-codec` provides a `Decode` trait which allows bytes to be scale decoded into types based on the shape of those
types. This crate builds on this, and allows bytes to be decoded into types based on type information, rather than the shape
of the target type. At a high level, this crate just aims to do the reverse of the `scale-encode` crate.

This crate exposes four traits:

- A `visitor::Visitor``visitor::decode_with_visitor`
- An `IntoVisitor``visitor::Visitor`
- A `DecodeAsType``IntoVisitor``scale_type_resolver::TypeResolver`
- A `DecodeAsFields``Field`

Implementations for many built-in types are also provided for each trait, and the [ DecodeAsType](https://docs.rs/derive.DecodeAsType.html) macro can be used to
generate the relevant impls on new struct and enum types such that they get a

[impl.](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsType.html)

`DecodeAsType`The [ DecodeAsType](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsType.html) and

[traits are basically the mirror of](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsFields.html)

`DecodeAsFields``scale-encode`’s `EncodeAsType` and `EncodeAsFields`
traits in terms of their interface.[§](https://docs.rs#motivation)Motivation

By de-coupling the shape of a type from how bytes are decoded into it, we make it much more likely that the decoding will succeed, and are no longer reliant on types having a precise layout in order to be decoded into correctly. Some examples of this follow.

```
use codec::Encode;
use scale_decode::DecodeAsType;
use scale_info::{PortableRegistry, TypeInfo};
use std::fmt::Debug;
// We normally expect to have type information to hand, but for our examples
// we construct type info from any type that implements `TypeInfo`.
fn get_type_info<T: TypeInfo + 'static>() -> (u32, PortableRegistry) {
    let m = scale_info::MetaType::new::<T>();
    let mut types = scale_info::Registry::new();
    let ty = types.register_type(&m);
    let portable_registry: PortableRegistry = types.into();
    (ty.id, portable_registry)
}
// Encode the left value statically.
// Decode those bytes into the right type via `DecodeAsType`.
// Assert that the decoded bytes are identical to the right value.
fn assert_decodes_to<A, B>(a: A, b: B)
where
    A: Encode + TypeInfo + 'static,
    B: DecodeAsType + PartialEq + Debug,
{
    let (type_id, types) = get_type_info::<A>();
    let a_bytes = a.encode();
    let new_b = B::decode_as_type(&mut &*a_bytes, type_id, &types).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(b, new_b);
}
// Start simple; a u8 can DecodeAsType into a u64 and vice versa. Numbers will all
// try to convert into the desired output size, failing if this isn't possible:
assert_decodes_to(123u64, 123u8);
assert_decodes_to(123u8, 123u64);
// Compact decoding is also handled "under the hood" by DecodeAsType, so no "compact"
// annotations are needed on values.
assert_decodes_to(codec::Compact(123u64), 123u64);
// Enum variants are lined up by variant name, so no explicit "index" annotation are
// needed either; DecodeAsType will take care of it.
#[derive(Encode, TypeInfo)]
enum Foo {
    #[codec(index = 10)]
    Something(u64),
}
#[derive(DecodeAsType, PartialEq, Debug)]
enum FooTarget {
    Something(u128),
}
assert_decodes_to(Foo::Something(123), FooTarget::Something(123));
// DecodeAsType will skip annotated fields and not look for them in the encoded bytes.
// #[codec(skip)] and #[decode_as_type(skip)] both work.
#[derive(Encode, TypeInfo)]
struct Bar {
    a: bool,
}
#[derive(DecodeAsType, PartialEq, Debug)]
struct BarTarget {
    a: bool,
    #[decode_as_type(skip)]
    b: String,
}
assert_decodes_to(
    Bar { a: true },
    BarTarget { a: true, b: String::new() },
);
// DecodeAsType impls will generally skip through any newtype wrappers.
#[derive(DecodeAsType, Encode, TypeInfo, PartialEq, Debug)]
struct Wrapper {
    value: u64
}
assert_decodes_to(
    (Wrapper { value: 123 },),
    123u64
);
assert_decodes_to(
    123u64,
    (123,)
);
// Things like arrays and sequences are generally interchangeable despite the
// encoding format being slightly different:
assert_decodes_to([1u8,2,3,4,5], vec![1u64,2,3,4,5]);
assert_decodes_to(vec![1u64,2,3,4,5], [1u8,2,3,4,5]);
```
If this high level interface isn’t suitable, you can implement your own [ visitor::Visitor](https://docs.rs/visitor/trait.Visitor.html)’s. These can support zero-copy decoding
(unlike the higher level

[interface), and generally the Visitor construction and execution is zero alloc, allowing for efficient type based decoding.](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsType.html)

`DecodeAsType`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- This is similar to `DecodeAsType``DecodeAsType`
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAsType.html)- AsType
- This trait is implemented for any type `T`where`T`implements`IntoVisitor``Visitor``Error``visitor::decode_with_visitor``scale-encode`’s`EncodeAsType`.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/trait.FieldIter.html)- Iter

Under the hood, the macro generates`scale_decode::visitor::Visitor`and`scale_decode::IntoVisitor`implementations for each type (as well as an associated`Visitor`struct), which in turn means that the type will automatically implement`scale_decode::DecodeAsType`.

# parity-scale-codec 3.7.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/parity-scale-codec/^3.0.0

# Parity SCALE Codec

Rust implementation of the SCALE (Simple Concatenated Aggregate Little-Endian) data format for types used in the Parity Substrate framework.

SCALE is a light-weight format which allows encoding (and decoding) which makes it highly suitable for resource-constrained execution environments like blockchain runtimes and low-power, low-memory devices.

It is important to note that the encoding context (knowledge of how the types and data structures look) needs to be known separately at both encoding and decoding ends. The encoded data does not include this contextual information.

To get a better understanding of how the encoding is done for different types,
take a look at the ["Type encoding (SCALE)" page in Substrate docs](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/scale-codec/).

## Implementation

The codec is implemented using the following traits:

### Encode

The `Encode` trait is used for encoding of data into the SCALE format. The `Encode` trait
contains the following functions:

- `size_hint(&self) -> usize`: Gets the capacity (in bytes) required for the encoded data. This is to avoid double-allocation of memory needed for the encoding. It can be an estimate and does not need to be an exact number. If the size is not known, even no good maximum, then we can skip this function from the trait implementation. This is required to be a cheap operation, so should not involve iterations etc.
- `encode_to<T: Output>(&self, dest: &mut T)`: Encodes the value and appends it to a destination buffer.
- `encode(&self) -> Vec<u8>`: Encodes the type data and returns a slice.
- `using_encoded<R, F: FnOnce(&[u8]) -> R>(&self, f: F) -> R`: Encodes the type data and executes a closure on the encoded value. Returns the result from the executed closure.

**Note:** Implementations should override `using_encoded` for value types and `encode_to` for
allocating types. `size_hint` should be implemented for all types, wherever possible. Wrapper
types should override all methods.

### Decode

The `Decode` trait is used for deserialization/decoding of encoded data into the respective
types.

- `fn decode<I: Input>(value: &mut I) -> Result<Self, Error>`: Tries to decode the value from SCALE format to the type it is called on. Returns an- `Err`if the decoding fails.

### CompactAs

The `CompactAs` trait is used for wrapping custom types/structs as compact types, which makes
them even more space/memory efficient. The compact encoding is described [here](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/scale-codec/#fn-1).

- `encode_as(&self) -> &Self::As`: Encodes the type (self) as a compact type. The type- `As`is defined in the same trait and its implementation should be compact encode-able.
- `decode_from(_: Self::As) -> Result<Self, Error>`: Decodes the type (self) from a compact encode-able type.

### HasCompact

The `HasCompact` trait, if implemented, tells that the corresponding type is a compact
encode-able type.

### EncodeLike

The `EncodeLike` trait needs to be implemented for each type manually. When using derive, it is
done automatically for you. Basically the trait gives you the opportunity to accept multiple
types to a function that all encode to the same representation.

## Usage Examples

Following are some examples to demonstrate usage of the codec.

### Simple types

```
# // Import macros if derive feature is not used.
#
# use ;
use ;
let a = A;
let b = B;
let c = C ;
a.using_encoded;
b.using_encoded;
c.using_encoded;
let mut da: & = b"\x0f";
assert_eq!;
let mut db: & = b"\x01\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0";
assert_eq!;
let mut dc: & = b"\x02\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0";
assert_eq!;
let mut dz: & = &;
assert_eq!;
#
```
### Compact type with HasCompact

```
# // Import macros if derive feature is not used.
#
# use ;
use ;
let test_val:  = ;
let encoded = Test1HasCompact .encode;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
#
```
### Type with CompactAs

```
# // Import macros if derive feature is not used.
#
# use ;
use ;
use ;
;
let a =  ;
let encoded = a.encode;
assert_eq!;
#
```
## Derive attributes

The derive implementation supports the following attributes:

- `codec(dumb_trait_bound)`: This attribute needs to be placed above the type that one of the trait should be implemented for. It will make the algorithm that determines the to-add trait bounds fall back to just use the type parameters of the type. This can be useful for situation where the algorithm includes private types in the public interface. By using this attribute, you should not get this error/warning again.
- `codec(skip)`: Needs to be placed above a field or variant and makes it to be skipped while encoding/decoding.
- `codec(compact)`: Needs to be placed above a field and makes the field use compact encoding. (The type needs to support compact encoding.)
- `codec(encoded_as = "OtherType")`: Needs to be placed above a field and makes the field being encoded by using- `OtherType`.
- `codec(index = 0)`: Needs to be placed above an enum variant to make the variant use the given index when encoded. By default the index is determined by counting from- `0`beginning wth the first variant.
- `codec(encode_bound)`,- `codec(decode_bound)`and- `codec(mel_bound)`: All 3 attributes take in a- `where`clause for the- `Encode`,- `Decode`and- `MaxEncodedLen`trait implementation for the annotated type respectively.
- `codec(encode_bound(skip_type_params))`,- `codec(decode_bound(skip_type_params))`and- `codec(mel_bound(skip_type_params))`: All 3 sub-attributes take in types as arguments to skip trait derivation of the corresponding trait, e.g. T in- `codec(encode_bound(skip_type_params(T)))`will not contain a- `Encode`trait bound while- `Encode`is being derived for the annotated type.

## Known issues

Even though this crate supports deserialization of arbitrarily sized array (e.g. `[T; 1024 * 1024 * 1024]`)
using such types is not recommended and will most likely result in a stack overflow. If you have a big
array inside of your structure which you want to decode you should wrap it in a `Box`, e.g. `Box<[T; 1024 * 1024 * 1024]>`.

License: Apache-2.0

# scale-bits 0.7.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/scale-bits/^0.7.0

This small utility crate provides two separate things:

- A `Bits`type that can be SCALE encoded and decoded, and is fully SCALE compatible with a`BitVec<u8, Lsb0>`. It's a deliberately simple type that is conceptually just a sequence of bools, and can be used as a replacement for`BitVec`when you don't need the additional complexity and functionality that it comes with. See the`bits`module for more.
- Utility methods to help encode and decode arbitrary bit sequences from their
SCALE representation, or skip over the corresponding bytes entirely, with zero
allocations. These bypass the need to first go via some `BitVec`with the right store/order type, and are WASM compatible (unlike`BitVec`'s`u64`store type). See the`scale`module for more.

These things play nicely together (ie you can encode and decode arbitrary bit
sequences directly into the `Bits` type), but don't need to be used together.

# scale-type-resolver 0.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/scale-type-resolver/^0.2.0

# scale-type-resolver

`scale-type-resolver` provides a generic `TypeResolver` trait which can be implemented for
any type that is capable of being given a type ID and resolving that into information about
how the type is SCALE encoded. This allows libraries like `scale-decode` to be able to decode
SCALE encoded bytes using either a modern type resolver like `scale_info::PortableRegistry`,
or using entirely custom type resolvers (which we would need in order decode blocks from pre-V14
metadata).

It's unlikely that you'd depend on this library directly; more likely you'd depend on a library
like `scale-decode` which uses and re-exports the `TypeResolver` trait itself.

This crate is `no_std` by default and doesn't require `alloc` except for tests.

---

"Small vector" optimization for Rust: store up to a small number of items on the stack

## Example

```
use ;

// This SmallVec can hold up to 4 items on the stack:
let mut v:  = smallvec!;
// It will automatically move its contents to the heap if
// contains more than four items:
v.push;
// SmallVec points to a slice, so you can use normal slice
// indexing and other methods to access its contents:
v = v + v;
v.sort;
```
